title: Generate Parentheses
description:
# Generate Parentheses

Given an integer `n`, generate every string that uses exactly `n` opening parentheses and `n` closing parentheses and is well formed.

A string is well formed when every prefix contains at least as many `(` characters as `)` characters, and the final counts of both characters are equal.

Return the combinations in any order.

## Example 1:

**Input:** n = 3
**Output:** ["((()))","(()())","(())()","()(())","()()()"]

## Example 2:

**Input:** n = 1
**Output:** ["()"]

## Constraints:

* `1 <= n <= 8`

tests.description: Two pairs produce the two Catalan combinations
Three pairs produce the five canonical combinations
Five pairs stress deeper nesting and concatenated blocks with forty-two combinations

solutions.name: Mutable Prefix Backtracking
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build one prefix at a time with a `StringBuilder`, tracking how many opening and closing parentheses have already been used. Add `(` while `open < n`, and add `)` only while `close < open`.

## Key Insight

The prefix rule is the whole legality test: a prefix can never have more closing parentheses than opening parentheses. Because every branch preserves that invariant, every completed string is valid, and every valid string is reachable.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(Cn * n), where Cn is the nth Catalan number and each returned string has length 2n.
- Space Complexity: O(n) recursion depth, excluding the output list.

solutions.name: Immutable String Backtracking
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the same open/close counters, but pass a new `String` to each recursive branch instead of mutating a shared builder. This makes each state self-contained and easy to inspect.

## Key Insight

The search tree is unchanged from mutable backtracking; the tradeoff is representation. Immutable prefixes are simpler for beginners, while the mutable route avoids repeated allocation on the path.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(Cn * n), with extra copying hidden in string concatenation.
- Space Complexity: O(Cn * n) across temporary and returned strings.

solutions.name: Iterative State Stack
solutions.description:
## Approach

Replace recursion with an explicit stack of states. Each state stores the current prefix plus the number of used opening and closing parentheses. Pop a state, expand its legal next states, and collect completed prefixes.

## Key Insight

Backtracking does not require the Java call stack. The explicit stack exposes the same state graph, which is useful when teaching recursion as a search process rather than a language feature.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(Cn * n).
- Space Complexity: O(Cn * n) in the explicit stack and produced strings.

solutions.name: Dynamic Programming by Catalan Split
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the decomposition `(` + left + `)` + right. If the left side uses `k` pairs, the right side uses `n - 1 - k` pairs. Build every `dp[i]` from earlier lists.

## Key Insight

Every valid parenthesis string has a first matching close for its first open parenthesis. That matching pair splits the string into two smaller valid strings, giving the Catalan recurrence.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(Cn * n), because all valid strings must be materialized.
- Space Complexity: O(Cn * n) for the dynamic-programming lists and output strings.

solutions.name: Bitmask Generate and Filter Baseline
solutions.description:
## Approach

Enumerate every bitmask of length `2n`, keep only masks with exactly `n` opening positions, and scan each candidate to reject any prefix whose balance drops below zero.

## Key Insight

This route is intentionally a correctness baseline. It separates generation from validation and makes the prefix-balance definition of a well-formed string completely explicit.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n * 4^n), because it inspects all length-2n masks.
- Space Complexity: O(n) working space, excluding the output list.
